flashcards.front: Margin vs markup: the key difference?
flashcards.back:
Same profit, different denominator. Margin divides by price, markup by cost.
30% margin = 42.9% markup.
Revenue minus all variable costs. What each sale adds towards fixed costs and profit.
A cost that changes because of the decision being made. Allocated overhead usually is not one.
What you actually keep after on-invoice discounts and off-invoice deductions (rebates, waivers, freight, free service).
Pocket price minus variable cost to serve the deal.
Step-by-step view from list price to pocket price and pocket margin, showing every deduction.
List price minus on-invoice discounts. Off-invoice items still have to come off it to reach pocket price.

flashcards.front: Movement along vs shift of the demand curve
flashcards.back: Along: your own price changes. Shift: something else changes (competitors, economy, marketing).
Volume changes less than price in % terms, so a price rise increases revenue.
Elasticity between two price points using midpoint % changes. Symmetric in either direction.
% change in your volume / % change in another product's price. Positive = substitutes, negative = complements.
% change in volume / % change in customer income. Shows exposure to the economic cycle.
The most an informed customer should pay: next best alternative, adjusted for differentiation value.
What the customer would realistically do instead. Its cost is the reference value in EVC.
The maximum a customer would pay. A distribution across customers, not one number.
Asks 'would you buy at £X?' at several prices. Gives a demand curve for one fixed offer.
Four questions: too cheap, bargain, expensive, too expensive. Gives an acceptable price range, not purchase likelihood.
Respondents choose between packages with varied attributes and prices. Reveals trade-offs and feature values.
Stated WTP exceeds real behaviour because no money is at stake. Calibrate against actual purchases.
A rule deciding who qualifies for a price, based on facts customers cannot easily fake. Prevents leakage and arbitrage.
Customers obtaining a lower price meant for another segment, or reselling across segments.
Tiered offers so customers self-select by need. Each tier should be a real, rational choice.
Fixed fee plus usage price, e.g. £300 origination + factor 1.235.
A new or cheaper option takes sales from your own higher-margin option rather than winning new customers.
One firm moves price first and others tend to follow. Lawful only without coordination.
Rounds of cuts and matching that lower prices for the whole market. Often triggered by misdiagnosed share loss.
Adjust for package, fees, terms, service and channel so you compare total cost like for like.
Allowed price range by deal type, often green / amber / approval-required bands above a hard floor.
Central team that approves out-of-policy deals and keeps exception discipline.
Every concession is traded for a customer commitment of similar value.
Pricing and allocating fixed, perishable capacity across time and customer types to maximise contribution.
Dynamic: reacts to market conditions, the same for everyone at that moment. Personalised: reacts to information about the individual.
Timing and depth of price cuts on perishable stock, trading margin against sell-through and leftover value.
A hard limit the pricing system cannot break: floor, maximum change, consistency rule, approval trigger.
An unmeasured factor drives both price and sales, distorting the estimated price effect.
Demand conditions set the price, rather than price driving demand, e.g. raising rates when demand is strong.
Compares the change in a treated group with the change in a control group. Assumes parallel trends.
A weighted combination of untreated units built to mimic the treated unit before the change.
The smallest true effect a test is designed to detect reliably. Drives sample size and duration.
Existing customers or contracts keep the old price for a defined period after a change.
Who is Responsible, Accountable, Consulted and Informed for each implementation task.
Implementation: the price was not applied as planned. Hypothesis: it was applied, but customers responded differently than predicted.
Observed / modelled with uncertainty / untested belief / deliberate decision. Label each in a recommendation.
Multiplier on the advance giving total repayable. 1.25 on £20,000 = £25,000. Fixed regardless of how quickly it is repaid.
Share of daily card takings remitted. A higher holdback means faster repayment and a higher effective annual cost.
Raising price drives away the lower-risk customers first, so expected loss per deal rises.
A new advance to an existing merchant, often once 50%+ is repaid. Lower acquisition cost and better data, so often priced lower.

explainCards.prompt: Why can a revenue-maximising price fail to maximise contribution?
explainCards.answer: Revenue ignores costs. A lower price can win enough extra volume to raise revenue, but each extra deal carries variable cost, so the margin per unit falls faster than volume grows. Example: fee £4,500 x 1,200 = £5.4m revenue but £1.2m contribution, vs £5,500 x 900 = £4.95m revenue and £1.8m contribution.

explainCards.prompt: Why does a 5% price rise increase unit contribution by much more than 5%?
explainCards.answer: Costs do not move, so the whole price rise drops into contribution. With a thin margin, £250 on a £1,500 contribution is +16.7%. The thinner the margin, the bigger the leverage, and the more volume you can afford to lose.

explainCards.prompt: Why can list price changes miss most of the profit opportunity?
explainCards.answer: Real money is lost between list and pocket price through discounts, rebates and waivers that vary deal by deal. If leakage is large and uneven, controlling it moves profit more than a list change, which also gets discounted away.

explainCards.prompt: Why can't you read elasticity straight off a before-and-after sales chart?
explainCards.answer: Other things change at the same time: seasonality, competitors, broker behaviour, marketing, capacity. A before-and-after comparison credits all of them to price. You need controls or a comparison group.

explainCards.prompt: For an MCA, why does the elasticity number depend on whether you measure the factor rate or the fee?
explainCards.answer: The same move (1.25 to 1.30) is +4% on the rate but +20% on the fee, so the elasticity differs five-fold. The fee is what the merchant actually pays for capital, so it is usually the better 'price'. Always state which one you use.

explainCards.prompt: Why is long-run elasticity usually larger than short-run?
explainCards.answer: Customers need time to find alternatives, renegotiate, or change behaviour. A price rise may look harmless for a month while the real volume loss builds as contracts end and brokers redirect deals.

explainCards.prompt: Why should price normally sit below EVC rather than at it?
explainCards.answer: At EVC a fully informed customer is indifferent, so they have no reason to switch, and real customers are not fully informed and doubt your claims. Leaving some value on the table gives them a reason to choose you.

explainCards.prompt: Why do survey answers about price often overstate what customers will actually pay?
explainCards.answer: No money is at stake (hypothetical bias), people want to seem reasonable, and some answer strategically. Real acceptance data shows the gap. Calibrate stated intent against past behaviour.

explainCards.prompt: What makes a price fence strong rather than leaky?
explainCards.answer: It relies on facts you can verify and the customer cannot fake or easily change: repayment history, turnover data, contract term, timing. Fences based on what customers say, or available on request, spread the discount to everyone.

explainCards.prompt: Why can adding more price options reduce sales?
explainCards.answer: Too many options slow decisions, confuse sales and brokers, and make the right choice unclear. Customers delay or default to the cheapest option. A few clear trade-offs usually beat many combinations.

explainCards.prompt: Why can matching a competitor's price cut destroy value even if you keep share?
explainCards.answer: You give the cut to every customer, including those who were not leaving. If the real cause of share loss was speed or service, the cut does not fix it, and rivals may cut again.

explainCards.prompt: Why is a competitor's headline rate a poor benchmark on its own?
explainCards.answer: Fees, holdback, term, service and eligibility differ. Normalising to total cost on the same deal often shrinks the gap. A £600 headline difference became £200 once the origination fee was added.

explainCards.prompt: Why do pricing policies fail if sales incentives stay volume-based?
explainCards.answer: Each discount helps the seller close and costs them nothing. Exceptions creep back, approvals become routine and realised price drifts down. Incentives tied to realised price or contribution align sellers with the policy.

explainCards.prompt: Why trade concessions instead of simply granting them?
explainCards.answer: A free discount teaches customers that pushing works and sets the next negotiation's starting point. Trading it for a commitment (faster holdback, renewal, volume) recovers value and makes asking for a discount costly.

explainCards.prompt: Why can raising price when capacity is full add profit without losing any funded volume?
explainCards.answer: If demand exceeds capacity, you turn customers away anyway. A higher price only removes customers you could not serve, so every funded deal earns more and volume does not fall.

explainCards.prompt: Why is personalised pricing riskier than dynamic pricing?
explainCards.answer: Dynamic prices are the same for everyone at a given moment and respond to observable conditions. Personalised prices depend on who you are, which raises discrimination, data-use and fairness concerns, especially if they target urgency or vulnerability.

explainCards.prompt: How can historical data show higher prices linked to more sales?
explainCards.answer: An omitted variable or reverse causality: riskier merchants get higher rates and have fewer alternatives, or prices are raised when demand is strong. The correlation reflects why price varied, not how customers respond to it.

explainCards.prompt: Why must the decision rule be written before the test starts?
explainCards.answer: Otherwise people pick whichever metric looks good after the fact. Pre-committing to the profit measure, MDE, guardrails and launch threshold keeps the test honest.

explainCards.prompt: Why separate implementation failure from a flawed pricing hypothesis?
explainCards.answer: They need opposite fixes. If the price was not applied, tighten execution. If it was applied and customers reacted more than expected, revisit the price. Without the breakdown you might reverse a good decision.

explainCards.prompt: What should repeated exceptions tell governance?
explainCards.answer: That the policy does not fit reality, or that controls are weak. Either way, review the policy rather than approving the same exception again and again.

explainCards.prompt: Why show a break-even condition alongside the scenarios?
explainCards.answer: It tells leaders the assumption value at which the decision stops paying, e.g. 'loss-making if volume falls more than 10.9%'. They can judge plausibility directly and know what to monitor.

explainCards.prompt: Why label facts, estimates, assumptions and choices separately?
explainCards.answer: It shows where the uncertainty really is, so challenge focuses on the right inputs and nobody mistakes a belief for a measured fact.

gross-margin-pct.interpretation: Price is the realised net price per unit. Cost is the direct cost per unit. Result as % of price.

markup-pct.interpretation: Same price and cost inputs as margin, so the two are directly comparable. Result as % of cost.

unit-contribution.interpretation: Net price minus every cost that varies with one more unit.

break-even-volume.interpretation: Fixed cost for the period divided by unit contribution. Rounded up to whole units when used as a target.

price-elasticity.interpretation: Two methods. Arc (midpoint), as used in the Week 2 exercise: %Δ = change / average of old and new. Simple: %Δ = change / old value. The arc method gives the same answer in both directions.

required-new-volume.interpretation: Assumes variable cost per unit is unchanged, as the syllabus states. Break-even volume change = required new volume / old volume - 1.

incremental-profit.interpretation: Total contribution after minus total contribution before, minus one-off implementation cost, over the same stated period.

initiative-roi.interpretation: Net ROI: incremental profit already has implementation cost subtracted, so the cost is not subtracted again.
